utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This case is IT-00-39 & 40-PT, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik, Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'll have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge May. I am Mark Harmon, appearing for the Prosecutor. Appearing with me is my colleague Mr. Alan Tieger, and to my left is Carmela Annink-Javier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Deyan Brashich, together with Nikola Kostich, for the Krajisnik Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. For the Plavsic Defence, Robert Pavich, with Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan and Mr. Peter Murphy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a Status Conference in this case. The matters to be addressed appear to be these, and of course I'll hear of any others: There are matters of timetabling. There are matters of outstanding disclosure, translation problems, matters of the exhibits including the videos, the disclosure of 11.000 and more documents, expert reports, and then agreed and adjudicated facts. Those have been identified by the Trial Chamber as matters which we ought to address at this Status Conference. The most expeditious way to deal with this may be to start with the Prosecution and start going through some of the issues, perhaps beginning, Mr. Harmon, if we may, with the disclosure and deal with the state of disclosure. To date, you have filed your pre-trial brief, witness list, and exhibit list. You've identified, as I understand it, 400 witnesses - slightly more - and you are going to apply for 200 of those to be put in in statement form.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as the witnesses are concerned, I anticipate there are no immediate matters to be dealt with. No doubt there will have to be rulings in due course, and we can perhaps come back to that in terms of a timetable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can apprise Your Honour that insofar as the witness statements are concerned, there were six witness statements that were not provided by the date of the filing of the pre-trial brief. Those witness statements are available today and will be provided to the Defence today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So dealing with -- perhaps while we're on the witnesses, that means that all the statements will be provided. In what language?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There are, I am informed, 26 newly-selected witnesses who appear on the witness list in the pre-trial brief. There are -- some of those statements are untranslated into B/C/S. They have been submitted to the Language Service Section for translation, and they will be provided in a language the accused understands as soon as we get them back from the Language Service Section. All of the rest of the statements have been provided to the Defence in a language the accused understands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And as far as Rule 92 bis is concerned, what are your plans in that direction?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let me give Your Honour a comprehensive report on the status of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 92 bis, as Your Honour is aware, is a process that includes going into the field and collecting a proper declaration from witnesses. We have been engaged in that time-consuming and resource-intensive and expensive endeavour for over a year, and we have and continue to engage in the process of collecting the proper declarations. I can tell Your Honour that the results of this prodigious effort have been mixed. We have identified 212 witnesses on our witness list of 406 as being 92 bis witnesses. That's 52 per cent of our witnesses in the trial, we propose to have their testimonies come in through written evidence, either under 92 bis (B), sub-part (C) or sub-part (D). To date, we have furnished the Defence with 103 statements under 92 bis. We have 13 new statements that we have collected in the field that are now being processed. They come from a mission that was completed on the 26th of April, 2002, and they will be submitted to the Defence once the processing of those statements is complete. We expect that to be very quickly done. There are 49 witness statements that remain to be collected, the proper declarations need to be collected. We anticipate that those missions will be completed by mid-July, and we will process those statements very quickly. Now, turning my attention, Your Honour, to the 103 92 bis statements that have been submitted to the Defence to date, the Krajisnik Defence informed me on the 9th of May, 2002, that they objected to all of the 103 statements taken under 92 bis and submitted to them on the basis that they were written statements that go to the proof of acts and conduct of the accused as charged in the indictment under 7(3). Now, they also noted in their letter to me that portions of those statements would be properly admitted under the provisions of 92 bis, but the Krajisnik Defence does not have time or resources to specify which part of each statement would not be objectionable. On the 6th of May, the Plavsic Defence advised me that 83 of those statements, of those 103 statements that have been submitted to them, would be accepted without reservation and 16 of those statements would be acceptable with redactions made. And I have not had time to discuss with my colleagues from the Defence those particular 16 statements, but I am quite confident that I and the Defence will reach some agreement on some of those statements. There was one statement under 92 bis that the Plavsic Defence objected to and three statements had not been disclosed to them in English, and therefore they were of no opinion. They could not give me an opinion as to those statements. So the results in respect of 92 bis are essentially divided. We have one defendant disagreeing on all; another defendant agreeing on a significant portion of them. It is our intention, Judge May, to file a motion with the Trial Chamber for the admission of 103 statements objected to by the Krajisnik Defence and possibly the one statement objected to by the Plavsic Defence. It is our intention to file with the Trial Chamber the list of the 83 statements for which the Plavsic Defence has no objection. We will file the list of those statements and the actual statements with the Trial Chamber, and we invite the Trial Chamber to give us a scheduling order as to when we should file our motion as to the 103 statements that are objected to by the Krajisnik Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with that now. When can you do it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would say, Your Honour, we could probably do that by a week from today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's 17th May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As I understand, the Defence at least have indicated to you their view about it, so they could respond fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, well, let's deal with that now. You hear the proposal for the Defence. You've given provisional views, informal views. Is there any reason why you shouldn't give some views to the Trial Chamber fairly rapidly on that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I'm quite sure that we can very rapidly respond to the 92 bis motion, especially since, with the witness list, we have been provided with the specific counts in the indictment that these 92 bis statements are being offered for.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Judge May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two weeks, three weeks? Three weeks. So the response in three weeks. And we will rule as far as possible on those matters. Yes, now, that leaves the remainder of 92 bis. What are your proposals there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, my proposal would be that the 13 new statements that have been completed we will get to the Defence, as I say, as soon as possible. I'm not quite sure how long it takes to do the processing, but I don't imagine it takes -- it should not take more than a few days to do the processing. We will submit those statements to the Defence, I would say, by the same date, by the 17th of May. And it would seem to me that they can give me their provisional views on those 13 statements rather quickly. On the 49 witness statements that remain to be taken, those will not be completed, as I have said, until mid-July. We will submit those to the Defence as quickly as we can process those statements, but it will be, I would think, probably late July or early August before we can submit those remaining 49 statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: By my mathematics, that comes out at about 175, something of that sort. You said you had 202 -- 212.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm told 212, and I will need to check the math. This is the advice I have received. And if you bear with me, I will have an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We understand that those outstanding, in any event, you will submit as soon as possible. We will leave the matter there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is obviously in hand. Let us now go on to the issue, other issues, of disclosure; in particular, the exhibits and the transcripts, videos, all those matters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I turn my attention first to the video clips, because these issues are all interrelated, and the issue of exhibits is interrelated to the issues of pre-trial resolution of matters before the case, because there's a direct impact on if the parties can agree, for example, on adjudicated facts or if they can agree on other issues, the exhibits go down considerably. So if I may, Judge May, I would like to address the issues of where we have made efforts to resolve these matters, and then turn my attention at the end to the number of exhibits. With the Court's indulgence, I will start in that fashion. I can say, Your Honour, that we have endeavoured over the period of time that we've had this -- that I've had this case to try to resolve issues by agreement. Let me turn my attention first to agreed-upon facts in the indictment. In an effort to reduce the scale and duration of the trial and reduce the number of exhibits in this case, I have proposed to the Defence that they take the indictment and take a colour marker and mark through the indictment and identify those portions of the indictment that are not in dispute. I was rebuffed on that proposal. The joint Defence position on this is that everything is in dispute, and, therefore, we have been unable to reduce the size and scale of the number of exhibits, and obviously that impacts on the translation backlog. So as far as agreed-upon facts in the indictment, there are none. Now, turning my attention to adjudicated facts, which also have a direct bearing on the size and scale of this case and the number of exhibits and also the translation backlog, there have been submitted to the Defence 1.363 adjudicated facts. There were four separate submissions of those facts to the Defence. The first was about 20 months ago --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... 2000, 537 facts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will. There were four separate submissions made to the Defence. The first, as I say, was about 20 months ago. It was on the 21st of September, 2000; it was a submission of 537 adjudicated facts. On the 14th of December, 2000, about 17 months ago, an additional 34 adjudicated facts were submitted to the Defence. Five months ago, on the 11th of December, 2001, an additional 408 adjudicated facts were submitted to the Defence. And on the 28th of March, 2002, an additional 384 adjudicated facts were submitted to the Defence. Now, as I say, those adjudicated facts were submitted to the Defence in order to streamline the trial and reduce the problems that now confront us. Now, the current status of that is that there has been no acceptance of any of those adjudicated facts by the Defence. I am assured by the Plavsic Defence separately that they will now devote their attention to this, and I accept their undertaking to do so, particularly in light of their efforts in respect of 92 bis. I have not had conversations with the Krajisnik Defence team in respect of the adjudicated facts, although we -- I should take that back. Let me retract that, because I've misspoken. I have had conversations with Mr. Brashich in respect of adjudicated facts, and he did endeavour to go and consult with his client in respect of some of those adjudicated facts, and what was reported to me, and I'll defer to Mr. Brashich on this, was that it was a time-consuming process. Now, I have a proposal, and that is that in three weeks' time, that the Defence address themselves to the 1.363 adjudicated facts and give me a reply on what their position is in respect of each of those facts. And at that point in time, I will be in a position to inform the Chamber what is accepted and what is not, and we can litigate the issue of adjudicated facts once I am fully apprised of the position of the Defence. So that's what I can report to Your Honour insofar as adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's pause there and try and resolve that aspect of it. Now, I turn to the Defence, and it's not satisfactory, in my view, that there are no agreed facts. I cannot believe that there is nothing in the indictment which is not susceptible of agreement. It was, and I speak for my own experience, which some will recognise, it was the fashion 50 years ago to enter criminal litigation and say the Prosecution had to prove everything, everything was in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. dispute, the Defence would prove nothing. I suggest that things have moved on since then and that courts are moving towards - and certainly this Tribunal should be moving towards - a position where only the matters which really are in dispute are put before the Court for its resolution. And it's particularly important in a case of this sort, that matters which are susceptible of agreement should be agreed. Now, this does not mean, of course, that matters which are genuinely areas of dispute have to be agreed. There is no question of the Court coercing parties into agreement. That, of course, is not the position at all. But at the same time, may I suggest that a good faith attempt should be made to agree on some basic things so that at least we can move forward on an agreed basis and really deal properly in the trial with the matters which are the central core issues. One case - not this one - I remember where even the grid references on a map were in dispute. It's not necessary to conduct litigation, I suggest, these days in that way. Now, I recognise there's a burden on everybody in the coming months, but we must get this trial on. Mr. Brashich, the proposal is that in three weeks you address yourselves to the adjudicated facts issue. That's a rather different one, but I suggest to you that you have a look again to see whether some matters can't be agreed between the parties at the very outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I concur with your position, Judge May, as to litigation. However, there is a totally different aspect to this litigation which has to be addressed. We did try a good-faith effort to reach a consensus on what is agreed and what is disagreed upon. However, as we are speaking as to the adjudicated facts, they are in English. On one hand, we have been bombarded and we continue to receive boxes and boxes of documents which require our attention. On the other hand, I went over to the Detention Unit, visited with my client to get his brief and his direction as to the adjudicated facts. Now, there's 1.363 facts. I tried to translate the adjudicated facts and discuss them with my client. During the course of an afternoon, we got through 15. There was a suggestion that we receive some aid from a B/C/S speaker who would sit and translate, because it's quite difficult for me to do it and at the same time act as an attorney and at the same time act as a translator. So for that reason, I just had to drop it and not go any further with it because we just do not have neither the resources nor the time, based on what we are getting from the Prosecution. We just received 12 boxes of documents before we came to The Hague. We haven't even had a chance to open those boxes and find out what is inside. So the Defence is stretched to the limit, and we don't know what to address first.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to have the Court left with the impression that we have taken and are taking an unreasoned position on these issues. I think our position has been from the beginning that at the appropriate time, we would address this. An amended indictment was filed at the beginning of this year. That indictment was not sufficiently specific to enable us to address the adjudicated facts. And so our understanding was that once the pre-trial brief had been filed, we would then take that, together with the amended indictment, sit down with counsel for the Prosecution and work through these matters. It is still our intent to do so. It was always our intent to do it with that time frame in mind. I simply don't want to leave the Court the impression that we are taking an unreasoned position on this. It is something that we feel we would like to address, and we feel this is the appropriate time to do it. I would ask my colleague Mr. Murphy, who was at the last 65 ter conference, where I was not present, to address a couple of more specific issues on that, with the Court's indulgence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position as stated by Mr. Harmon, with great respect, with -- about the agreements on the adjudicated facts is somewhat incomplete. And if Your Honour would look at the transcript of the last 65 ter conference, I think that would become very clear. There were two matters of discussion: The first was, are there any facts in the indictment which could be admitted or agreed to? Mr. Harmon suggested, as he told the Court, that what we do is take a coloured pen and mark certain areas of the indictment which might be agreed and which were not. And he cited, for example, surely the defendants don't dispute their dates of birth. My response to that at the 65 ter conference was we will be very happy to sit down with you and discuss that, but there are two problems, both of which since probably have been resolved. One was that, at that time, we had not received the pre-trial brief. The second was that there was still an application for leave to appeal pending in the Appeals Chamber regarding the Trial Chamber's granting of leave to amend the consolidated indictment. We took the position that until those issues were resolved, it would be foolhardy of us to try to indicate agreed facts. Now that those matters are resolved, we stand by the promise we made to Mr. Harmon at the 65 ter conference to sit down with him and resolve the issue, and we will. Your Honour, as to the adjudicated facts, there was discussion of that matter at the 65 ter conference, and the transcript reflects that it was specifically agreed, I believe at the suggestion of Ms. Featherstone, that a timetable be established for that today at this Status Conference. And again, we have told Mr. Harmon on more than one occasion that we have reviewed most of the adjudicated facts. We anticipate that most of them will not be controversial. And it is our intention to respond positively, as I believe the Plavsic has always demonstrated, for example, in relation to the 92 bis statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let us consider how we move forward on this issue. Is there any practical reason why you shouldn't meet after this hearing and at least begin a preliminary discussion on this issue with the Prosecution? Is the Prosecution ready to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can I invite the Defence to meet with the Prosecution and at least begin preliminary discussions on trying to resolve these issues. The next proposal, clearly we should move towards a resolution; the earlier, the better. The proposal is that you respond in three weeks to the suggestion, suggestions made by the Prosecution. Now, that's the proposal. I'll hear your reaction to it, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Could I just confer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, after consulting, I just can't see how we can do it. We have been allotted a certain amount of hours, which we have used up. After discussing this with Mr. Kostich, with what we have on our plate, I just can't see having the time to, first, go into the decisions and the judgments, pulling those adjudicated facts and comparing them as they appear in the judgment and still have time to sit with Mr. Krajisnik and still attend to the other problems and other matters that we have before us. I just can't see it being done in three weeks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When do you think you could do it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: End of June, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let me consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, depending on which way the Court rules and schedules, we are at the same time also doing our pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I have that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And addressing the 12 boxes which we haven't opened yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that we have to come to a comprehensive timetable on all these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Plavsic Defence will comply with whatever date the Court decides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I will consider that. But the first matter is there should be a meeting after this hearing to try and start moving that matter along.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And I'm told the judgements are in B/C/S. Is that right, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. When we submitted the adjudicated facts to the Defence, we identified the particular paragraph from the judgement that we were extracting the adjudicated fact. And the judgements themselves are in B/C/S, and those judgements have been provided to the Defence. At least, some of those judgements have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: That's correct. Some of the judgements were, and I carry about 25 pounds of paper to the Detention Unit. And I also gave my client the English version of the adjudicated facts, and I left him with the chore to go through just using the numerical paragraphs. And I must admit I have not had a chance to get a report from my client as to how much of that he has completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt that's something which could be looked at today. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Turning my attention to the expert reports that have been filed with the Court, in June, early June of 2001, and on the 19th of October, 2001, we filed 16 exhumation reports, the statements of experts relating to these exhumation reports. Nine of those are translated into English; seven were untranslated; and all of those reports were given to the Defence on the dates I've informed Your Honour of. Now, in order to alleviate the translation bottleneck that is bedevilling us constantly in this case, a joint Defence expert was appointed to review all of the untranslated reports. On the 8th of March, 2002, the Krajisnik Defence filed a request to cross-examine all of the Defence experts. I was somewhat taken aback by that request, given that there had been a previous communication saying that the expert was not in a position to give an opinion unless and until he had received colour photographs relating to some of those exhumation reports. And I inquired as to whether or not those -- the expert could -- whether the expert -- I'm sorry. Whether the filing by the Krajisnik Defence applied to all of the expert reports or only those expert reports that did not have photographs at all. I also suggested that we should sit down and have -- identify what areas the expert had in disagreement, because we might be able to resolve issues to the expert's satisfaction. And I have not had any answer on that request. At the last 65 ter conference, the issue of these expert reports was raised and the joint position, the joint Defence position, was that all of the expert reports are contested, including the individual autopsy reports contained in those exhumations. Now, the impact on that, obviously, of that decision is considerable. It will create additional problems in terms of the translation backlog. We will submit those additional reports that are now being contested into the translation queue. And in addition to the 16 exhumations I've identified, we have an additional six exhumation reports that we intend to file that relate to additional sites identified in the indictment. So that is what I can report insofar as the 94 bis statements of experts, specifically the forensic experts dealing with exhumations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, whenever I appear here, there appears to be an onus on the Defence to do more than what it is doing. When we found ourselves with the problem that there were nine untranslated expert witness reports and they were given to us a year and a half or two years into this case, we went out of our way, both the Plavsic Defence and the Krajisnik Defence, to appoint a B/C/S-speaking expert to be able to get through the reports and to allow us to take a position. We have consulted with our expert, and based on our consultation, we have taken the position that we do not accept the expert witness report and we wish to cross-examine the particular witness. I know that we have a problem with translation, but that onus is not upon us. That onus is either on the Prosecution or the Registry. And I think that the Krajisnik Defence has tried to cooperate and be as reasonable as possible. And then, of course, we do stand by our position that we do wish to cross-examine the expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But, Mr. Brashich, what possible issues arise about exhumations?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: One very simple one is date of death. We have an indictment from June 1991 to December 30, 1992. Don't you think date of death is relevant, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't address the Trial Chamber like that. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Brashich, you see, here is a matter which it does seem to me should be susceptible of agreement. These are experts, I take it, and I take it they're independent. The notion -- I'm told, and that may be wrong, that there are some 70 or 80 individual autopsy reports. Now, it does seem to me again that this must be an area in which there could be some agreement. Now, what about, again, you can meet with the Prosecution to discuss what the issues are that arise. The notion that a Trial Chamber is going to spend a very long time going through that is a matter of concern. There are far more fundamental problems in this case. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've just been told --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're more than happy to meet, but I'll defer to Mr. Pavich on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: I think the Court's anticipated exactly what we plan Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to do. I think that with regard to the autopsy reports, it's a matter of our being able to establish a sufficient foundation that will reassure us that these reports relate to deaths that occurred within the period of indictment, and I believe that counsel for the Prosecution will sit down with us, and we will go through the materials that will address our concern as to what foundational material will be supplied in addition to the autopsies that will give us the assurance that these autopsies relate to deaths that occurred within the period of the indictment; I think precisely what the Court has in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I mean, it may be -- it may not be a matter which is susceptible, because it may not be a matter on which experts can agree. But of course there are procedures in some courts for experts to meet and, if necessary, to produce an agreed report. I don't know whether that's a way forward here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to make it clear that this is only one of the issues which our expert has raised. I have discussed these reports at length with Professor Dunjic, and it is based on his advice and not my independent decision or judgement that cross-examination was well warranted in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, meet with the Prosecution to see whether these matters can't be ironed out. I mean, if there are genuine matters of concern about the reports, then of course they should be addressed. But if they're peripheral and unimportant on analysis, then the report should be agreed as far as possible. So, Mr. Harmon, could you add to the agenda for the meeting something of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I will be glad to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Something of that aspect. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Turning now to the issue of video clips. In November of 2001, on the 6th of November, in an effort to alleviate the bottleneck on translations in respect of video clips that had been submitted to the Defence, the Defence undertook to have translated and prepared transcripts of video clips where no transcripts existed. Now, despite being assured repeatedly that the work had been done or some work had been done on these transcripts and that they would be provided to the Prosecution forthwith, to date we have not received any transcripts of video-clip material that has been apparently prepared in the former -- in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So that is what I can report insofar as the video clips are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the Krajisnik Defence undertaking and the only thing I can say is mea culpa. I have not followed through. Every time I wish to follow through and to call Belgrade and say, "Just put them in an envelope and send them," I get derailed. I was thinking of going to Belgrade tomorrow. If not, I will get the transcripts that have been done. And as I have advised Ms. Featherstone in several Rule 65 ter conferences, that effort came to a dead stop due to lack of resources. But what has been done, if I have to personally deliver it, I will do it, but it is my mistake. Mea culpa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is the position that the transcripts have been completed and are waiting delivery or that they haven't been done?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: They have been done. They need to be polished, the ones that have been done, and delivered. But it's only a portion of the video clips, because we came to a stop due to resources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, seven days for return?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Seven days for return, and the video clips which haven't been processed should also be returned. Is that right, Mr. Harmon? Do you want the video clips back or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I would like the video clips back, and I would like the portion -- the clips clearly identified as to which -- I'm sorry, the transcripts for the clips clearly identified. So there would be a transcript from a clip that would be identified. We have given the Defence a list of the video clips with numbers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- and if they can correspond the transcript to the list that I have furnished to the Defence, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. Seven days, then. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now let me -- and I can turn my attention then to experts, the remaining experts. That appears on Your Honour's list, and let me address that issue. We have identified in our pre-trial brief some of the experts we intend to call, specifically Mr. Ewan Brown, Mr. Rick Butler, Pat Trenor, Professor Bianchini, and we have apparently omitted to identify, but I will identify now, two experts in addition; Robert Donia and Dolly Hanson. Those expert reports that are being prepared by these experts we will try to complete as soon as possible. I say that because some of these experts have very busy schedules. We have -- some of these expert reports are works in progress, and as I have said before, we will turn these expert reports over as soon as they are completed. There is an issue of two experts, a propaganda expert, which we have yet to identify. We have tried to identify the proper expert, and we have been unsuccessful to date in identifying that expert, but we continue in that effort. And the other expert is demographics. Again, we have been in consultation but have not yet identified the actual expert. We will continue to do so with great attention, and once identified, we will identify the expert to the Defence and have the reports turned over to the Defence as soon as we get the reports in hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. I seem to remember that experts feature in the motion which has been put forward by Mrs. Plavsic to exclude evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. We received that late yesterday afternoon, midday, and we will address more fully the issue of experts in our written reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, I think that probably leaves outstanding the matter of exhibits and translation. Perhaps you can update the Court on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to defer to my colleague Mr. Tieger to address this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course it's no accident that the Court mentioned those two issues in tandem. They are intertwined, and our discussions related to them have always taken place in recognition of that fact. I would draw the Court's attention, therefore, back to the last 65 ter conference, during which the translation project was discussed. At that time, all the parties strongly endorsed the project and expressed their support for it and the fact that they were greatly encouraged by it. We did identify a problem that the translation resource needed to be augmented in order to keep up with the capacity for review that had been created. At that conference, we assured your senior legal officer that we would direct our attention to that issue, and we have done so. With the tremendous cooperation within the institution, we have indeed augmented the translation capacity by a substantial percentage, greatly increased it, so that the output of translations will go from hundreds -- a few hundred pages a month to actually thousands of pages per month. And we are -- that process is being put in place. As of today, the first reinforcements will be on line today, and within a matter -- they will be consistently increased over the next few weeks. And the capacity I just described for thousands of pages, rather than hundreds, will be available shortly. I think that's the most direct and effective way of addressing the problem that we have been discussing up to now and satisfies the concerns of the parties as expressed at the 65 ter conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the current position? Can you update the Court as to the current position of documents untranslated? I am told, as I said, that the list contains over 11.000. Have they all been disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they have. The particular numbers involved are as follows: There are somewhat less than 7.800 exhibits. They total approximately 10.800 documents. Obviously, certain exhibits are a series of documents that relate closely to each other. I'm advised that there are approximately 4.500 documents awaiting translation, and those will be processed through the translation project. As I said, the logistical steps have already been put in place to ensure that the reinforced resources that have now been made available will be fully employed at all times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that I understand the position, the translation, is that from B/C/S into English and French?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Excuse me, Your Honour, I misspoke; into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Into English. Yes, well, that clearly is a serious matter we'll have to consider in due course, along with the motion. If this trial is to come on in October and November, which it really must, then we need to address that problem. But you're having them translated at the rate of a thousand a month. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Several thousand pages, Your Honour. Let me say that the resource allocation is geared to the number of pending documents and to the pending deadline. And we're augmenting that with that in mind in order to ensure that the deadline will be met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Harmon, one matter: Is the -- it would be sensible, right, to put a date for the expert reports? I have in mind a final cutoff point. Do you want to address me on that? You've explained your position, but there must come a time when the evidence is in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. In order to address you comprehensively, I need to consult with the experts themselves. And I would request that I address you either in a written memorandum or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you could have a memorandum within 14 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: On the availability of the experts' reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the date. Are there any matters which are outstanding as far as the Prosecution are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me turn to the Defence. The pre-trial brief has now been filed. A motion has been filed by Mrs. Plavsic which the Trial Chamber as a whole will have to consider. It's not a matter for me alone. And of course, we'll do so when we've had the response from the Prosecution. If necessary, we'll have to have an oral hearing on it. But meanwhile, I would wish to make a timetable towards a trial in the autumn, which has always been the ambition -- the proposal, rather. And what is required, of course, at the next stage is Defence responses. I've heard about that, adjudicated facts, and also the pre-trial briefs. And a tentative date, I think, has been set for the 1st of September, and that would allow the trial to start in October or November. But I'll hear the Defence as to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has always been our intent to do whatever is possible in order to bring this case to trial as quickly as possible. Our motion, I think, at this point speaks for itself. It raises some very grave concerns about whether we're going to be able to adequately prepare a defence within the time frame that we have all been working toward, and that is an October or November trial date. I think that we've heard now for the first time from counsel for the Prosecution that the seemingly insurmountable problem that we are confronted with, that is the problem of translation, is going to be addressed once again with a new approach, which sounds, based on past experience, to us at this point as being seen very optimistically by the Prosecution. I would suggest that we have a Status Conference within a reasonably short amount of time in order for us to determine how realistic the proposal that we have heard this morning for the first time, that is, that thousands of pages will now be translated per month as opposed to the trickle, literally, of less than 100 a month that we have been getting over the last several months because, Your Honour, it is impossible for us to make the kind of commitment that we want to make to the Court with regard to our pre-trial obligations without addressing this translation problem which, frankly speaking, has grown over the past several months. Rather than having this matter being more streamlined over the past several months, despite the encouragement of the Court, we found that the number of documents and exhibits that we have been confronted with has grown from last summer from the 800 core documents to a matter of now thousands, 10.000 documents, almost 5.000 of which have not been translated, which means probably 15 to 20.000 pages of documentation. And so on the one hand, while we have been aggressively trying to meet the problem, from the Plavsic Defence point of view, for example, bringing in 19 translators in Novi Sad on the project that has been proposed and put in effect over the past several months in an effort to deal with this translation problem, we are also then confronted with additional documents that we were given with the filing of the pre-trial brief. So that we will do everything we can to meet the Court deadlines. But I think realistically it is going to be impossible for us to make that commitment unless we can determine that this proposal that we've heard for the first time today is, in fact, a realistic proposal. Will the institution be able to go from translating less than a hundred pages a month to several thousand per month? Perhaps a Status Conference in the next two to three weeks will enable us to assess that and put us in a position where we can give a more realistic response to the Court. Because at this time, Your Honour, I'm not going to reiterate what's in the motion, but I think it's rather clear from our motion that we're not only at this point confronted with a less-than-perfect trial but a situation that may not allow us to meet our obligations under Articles 20 and 21. On the other hand, if this proposal is, in fact, realistic and we are going to be getting thousands of pages per month, we should get some sense of that within the next three to four weeks. And I would suggest a Status Conference so that we will be able at that point to more realistically assess the position that we can take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pavich, what I would have in mind is to fix a date of the pre-trial brief for the 1st of December [sic], with leave to apply to amend, if necessary, so that if you were unable to meet it, you could apply. But it is most important, in the Court's view, that this case comes on and that everything must be done towards that end, and for that reason, the target date for a Defence pre-trial brief will be of assistance, even with the difficulties which you've mentioned. But again, it may be sensible to discuss with the Prosecution, when you meet after this hearing, how the problem can be alleviated with regard to translation. Nobody wants the Defence to be in a position of simply being unable to prepare properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: That seems to be a reasonable position that the Court's encouraging us to take. I would ask the Court, however, to seriously scheduling a Status Conference in the reasonably near future so that we can again address this situation from a more realistic perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we will do that. Yes, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to make it clear that the Krajisnik Defence has joined the motion made by the Plavsic Defence with a reservation of rights which I filed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. I'll consult with the legal officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The orders we shall make with regard to the calendar are these: We will have a Status Conference on the 31st of May. It will have to be after the hearings in Milosevic. It will be at 12.00 or perhaps a bit later but on that day, the Friday. The Defence to respond with regard to adjudicated and agreed facts by the end of June, the 30th of June. The pre-Defence brief -- pre-trial brief, I should say, for the Defence, rather, the 1st of September. It's come up on the transcript on the last occasion as "December." Either, to use the expression of the Tribunal, I misspoke or it was taken down wrong, but 1st of September. And I encourage counsel to try and agree as much as possible, in a meeting hereafter, on those matters which have been discussed today. Also, it may be possible, Mr. Harmon, to do something at least with regard to the Plavsic motion, at least to try and resolve some of the issues. And perhaps we could have a report to the senior legal officer on any matters which have been agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are there any other matters which counsel want to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you for your attendance. We will adjourn until the 31st of May or the next date.
